blocks.text: Imagine trying to predict the exact height of a randomly chosen adult. While you can't pinpoint an exact number, you can describe the likelihood of different ranges using continuous random variables.

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore continuous random variables, which are used to model outcomes that can take any value within a given range. Unlike discrete random variables, continuous random variables are characterized by probability density functions (PDFs), which describe the relative likelihood of different outcomes.

blocks.title: Continuous Random Variable
blocks.text: A continuous random variable is a variable that can take any value within a given range. It is described by a probability density function (PDF), which specifies the probability of the variable falling within a particular range of values.

blocks.markdown: The key feature of a continuous random variable is that the probability of it taking any single, exact value is zero. Instead, we calculate the probability that it falls within an interval by integrating the PDF over that interval.

blocks.markdown: A common example of a continuous random variable is the normal distribution, which is symmetric and characterized by its mean ($\mu$) and standard deviation ($\sigma$).

blocks.title: Standard Normal Distribution
blocks.text: The standard normal distribution is a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. It is often denoted as $Z$.
